content.title: How to Watch the 2026 Boston Marathon
content.text: Published April 17, 2026 04:13PMThe 2026 Boston Marathon is finally here, and the elite field is stacked. Last year, Sharon Lokedi of Kenya shattered the course record, winning in 2:17:22. She returns this year with a pretty good chance of winning back-to-back. On the men’s side, Kenya’s John Korir will see if he can repeat his win as well. But don’t count the Americans out just yet. Their depth and positivity is hard to ignore. Can one of them make a move and get on the podium this year? Related: How to Watch the 2026 Boston Marathon With three recent American Olympians on the start list and a determined U.S. men’s squad (including Olympian Clayton Young and Zohair Talbi, who just ran a 2:05.45 in the Houston Marathon), there’s plenty of reason for excitement. We asked some of the athletes what’s been on their minds heading into Monday. Here’s a look inside the field. The following interviews have been edited for length and clarity. Sara Hall (USA) On running five marathons in five months: “I’ve just learned to rebound and re-enter and refocus on the next [marathon] as quickly as I can, but it’s really listening to your body. You want to take a little more rest than you feel like you need, because you don’t want to have to be taking it later. It’s an art I’ve been perfecting my whole marathon career.” And what she’s most looking forward to in the race: “Just enjoying the feeling of being out there. It’s going to be a nice cold day. I’ve been waiting for a day like this. And also, the feeling of the crowd… I don’t know how many more elite marathons I’m going to have, so what I know I’m going to miss is just that feeling of being out there.” Sharon Lokedi (KEN) Her self-talk while running: “When I’m starting I’m like, ‘Be patient, be patient.’ Then as we go I’m like, ‘Okay, it’s time to go, time to unleash yourself.’ It gets different as we go, but I always try to remember to be myself, be competitive, be present, and just enjoy the ride.” Training in Kenya with her family: “I was home for most of the time off, and it was amazing just being with family and enjoying that downtime. The whole week I’m busy with training and everything—it’s very tiring, you’re so dead almost every day. But then you get home and get to see your family, and they just help you come down. You almost forget the stress you had before.” Jess McClain (USA) On treating marathons like runcations: “I love adopting that mentality. Of course, I’m here because I’ve worked hard, and I’m taking the race seriously, but I think it’s also important to celebrate getting here. I used to think I could only have a good race if I locked myself away in my hotel room, legs up, feet up all weekend. But that was kind of stripping the joy from the whole experience.” Comparing last year’s race—where she finished seventh overall and first American—to this year: “Last year was so special. Sometimes you look back at a race where things went really well and you think, how can I replicate that? But I think it’s also important to recognize that every race is so different. The field is different, the weather is different. “So I’m leaning into the fact that it’s basically an American Championship wrapped into a world major. I’m really excited to toe the line with the best American women and the best international women, and just see what the 2026 version of me can do. Carpe diem.” Fiona O’Keeffe (USA) O’Keeffe shattered Molly Seidel’s American NYCM course record from 2021. (Photo: Derek Call ) On resetting after the New York City Marathon, where she finished fourth overall with the fastest-ever American time on the course: “After a big race like that, you definitely have to respect the toll it takes on your body. I had two weeks completely off of running, then slowly built back into it. [I] started workouts sometime in December, and it’s been a good training block since then. I was able to get out on the marathon course here at the end of January, which was really helpful, and then spent about the last five weeks up at altitude in Albuquerque.” RELATED: The (Mostly) Unspoken Rules of the Boston Marathon Jacket Why the Boston Marathon is special: I was able to be here for marathon weekend a few years ago, but I was racing the 5k. I watched from that corner on Boylston and I was like, ‘Okay, that’s what I want to do. It’s the marathon.’ So I’m so grateful to be here and have the opportunity to be a part of this field.” Galen Rupp (USA) On his goals for this race after running 2:09:41 in Chicago last October: “For me, the biggest thing is just continuing to improve over what I did in the fall. When those big breakthroughs happen, those are always great, but as long as you’re getting better every day in training and in every race, those are great signs.” On a strong build: “Staying healthy is the biggest thing when you’re training for a marathon. My health has been a lot better, my mechanics have been getting better, and my speed work has been a lot better than before Chicago last year. Before Chicago I felt like I hit a bit of a plateau with that, but it’s been a lot better for this build, so I’m really excited.” Emily Sisson (USA) Emily Sisson (left), Fiona O’Keeffe (middle) and Dakotah Popehn, née Lindwurm (right) celebrate after qualifying for the 2024 Paris Olympics at the U.S. Olympic Trials marathon on February 3 in Orlando, Florida. (Photo: Joe Hale) On her New England roots: “Living in Rhode Island through college and most of my 20s, I came here to preview the course, and I just remember thinking while running on it ‘it feels like Rhode Island, it feels nice, it feels clear.’ It’s challenging, and it was good to see because you need to prepare for that.” And her training block: “I used altitude for the first half of the build and did a lot of hills training up there, then came down with the goal to freshen up. I had a couple little setbacks in the second half of the build, but I think I still got enough freshening up in my legs while maintaining enough mileage.” Susanna Sullivan (USA) About her students’ excitement, knowing their teacher is a pro runner: “They’ve been really invested, and they’ve been really excited about the racing. But I also feel like as I move through [the] taper, I get more energetic. I think I am a little lighter and more fun. And so I feel like this last week at school, they were like, ‘It’s almost Marathon Monday!’ So, we had a lot of fun in class this week.” Zohair Talbi (USA) On coming to Boston after winning the Houston Marathon in January: “Houston was a great race. It was the first time I ran 2:05. It was an amazing feeling. Quickly after that I got back to training, knowing that Boston is still something I want to do. Since then I’ve just been building training well and staying healthy. I’m definitely taking that result and building off of it, and hopefully we get something better on Monday.” Clayton Young (USA) On missing Conner Mantz, who’s out due to injury: “Getting here is all about logistics—run, eat, sleep, meetings. A lot of little things that add up. My girls got in late last night, seven and five years old, and I’m excited to show them Boston. They’ve never been here, and they don’t get to travel to Dad’s races very often, so it’s going to help keep me grounded. I actually lucked out and was on the same flight as Conner, and we sat across the aisle from each other. But then I got on my first run, and he’s got his own schedule, his own thing. Usually, I have Keira D’amato or Conner to run with on these shakeout runs, to kind of fill the void of your mind on race weekend when there are a lot of voices. I was honestly kind of missing him out there. We like to strategize, we like to plan, we like to dream about what we want to do on race day.” Clayton Young runs behind his friend and training partner Conner Mantz at his home in Utah. (Photo: Gabriel Mayberry ) On faith and race weekend: “Faith is a daily choice. Trying to have an overall sense of gratitude and a prayer of thanks in my heart for just being healthy and being able to do what I love. During taper you’re filling the void of less miles and trying to get the mind right, and having a faith-based approach helps a lot. With the race being on Monday, I get to attend church on Sunday. There’s a little congregation here in Boston I’ve been attending the last few years, it’s kind of fun because all the members visiting will come and the congregation doubles in size. There are BYU alumni, friends, family, people I see every year just by going to church. It’s very grounding the day before a race. The other day I was doing strides on the indoor track and a gentleman pulled me aside and said, ‘That last 10k—just pray and push.’ And I think that’s really what the last 10k is all about. There’s no strategy at that point. It’s just get to the finish line, however ugly it may be.”
